overview: The Heian period was the high age of the Japanese court. With the Fujiwara regents running politics from Heian-kyo, the aristocracy turned to poetry, calligraphy and romance, and its women wrote the first great works of Japanese prose.

items.text: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.
Sei Shonagon finished The Pillow Book, her lists and observations of court life.
The kana syllabaries took shape, so that Japanese could be written without Chinese.
The Phoenix Hall of Byodoin at Uji was built for the Fujiwara, with its Amida by the sculptor Jocho.
Saicho founded Tendai on Mount Hiei and Kukai brought Shingon from China, the esoteric schools of the court.
Genshin's Essentials of Rebirth spread devotion to Amida Buddha and the Pure Land.
The sensibility of mono no aware, the pathos of passing things, ran through court writing.
Aristocratic life turned on poetry contests, music, calligraphy, incense and love affairs conducted by letter.
Court women, writing in kana, produced the diaries and tales that define the age.
The Tale of Genji remains at the center of Japanese literature.
The kana syllabaries are still the core of Japanese writing.

fall.text: The Minamoto destroyed the Taira in the Genpei War, ending at Dan-no-ura in 1185; Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled from Kamakura and was named shogun in 1192.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heian Period (794 to 1185)
